summary: Carney signs a strategic partnership with Turkey as Canada looks beyond the U.S., and Toronto's mayoral race looks close ahead of Monday's municipal vote.
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan launched a Canada-Türkiye strategic partnership in Ankara on Thursday, with a three-year action plan covering trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and ties between people [^1]. It is the first bilateral visit to Turkey by a Canadian prime minister [^2]. Erdogan said trade between the two countries is about $3 billion and should rise to $5 billion and then $10 billion, and that free-trade talks would start before the end of the year; officials will hold a first round in Ankara next month [^1]. Energy ministers will work on liquefied natural gas, nuclear power and critical minerals [^1]. "Our goal is not self-sufficiency; it is collective resilience," Carney said [^1]. The trip is part of his push to reduce Canada's reliance on the U.S. during the tariff dispute [^1][^2].

Amnesty International urged Carney to raise human rights, pointing to the jailing of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, a main Erdogan rival, for more than a year on corruption charges he denies, and to arrests of journalists and activists [^2]. Turkey's government says its courts are independent [^2]. Canada lifted a ban on weapons exports to Turkey in 2024 [^2].

Closer to home, Ontario holds municipal elections on Monday, Oct. 26. In Toronto, recent polls show a close race for mayor between Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford: Mainstreet Research had Bradford at 48.9% and Chow at 47.5%, while Pollara had Chow ahead 53% to 46% among decided voters [^3]. Both promise to get rid of TTC slow zones, and they have clashed over how to deal with bad landlords [^3]. In Ottawa, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said the federal budget will be tabled Nov. 5; the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects a $63.3-billion deficit for 2026-27 [^4].
differences: On Turkey, both governments present the partnership as a way to build resilience and trade [^1]; Amnesty International says Canada must not treat human rights as secondary to trade, while Turkey's government says its courts are independent [^2].
